questions.q: A sample of size \(n=49\) has mean \(\bar{x}=44\), drawn from a population with \(\mu_0=47\) and known \(\sigma=10\). Find the test statistic \(z\), correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.answer: Final Answer: -2.10. Working through this statistics step: \(z=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}=\frac{44-47}{10/\sqrt{49}}\approx -2.10\)
questions.explanation: Working through this statistics step: \(z=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}=\frac{44-47}{10/\sqrt{49}}\approx -2.10\)

questions.q: Evaluate \( \cos\left(\sin^{-1}\left(0\right)\right) \).
questions.answer: **Answer:** D. Working through this functions step: \( \text{Let }\theta=\sin^{-1}(0)\text{, so }\sin\theta=0\text{. Then }\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=1. \) [M1] [A1]
questions.explanation: Working through this functions step: \( \text{Let }\theta=\sin^{-1}(0)\text{, so }\sin\theta=0\text{. Then }\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=1. \) [M1] [A1]

questions.q: Evaluate \( \cos\left(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right) \).
questions.answer: **Answer:** A. Working through this functions step: \( \text{Let }\theta=\sin^{-1}(\dfrac{1}{2})\text{, so }\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{. Then }\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{4}}. \) [M1] [A1]
questions.explanation: Working through this functions step: \( \text{Let }\theta=\sin^{-1}(\dfrac{1}{2})\text{, so }\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{. Then }\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{4}}. \) [M1] [A1]

questions.q: A sample of size 100 from a population (known \(\sigma=20\)) gives \(\bar{x}=142\). Find a 99% CI for \(\mu\) and state what "99% confidence" means.
questions.answer: \(142\pm2.576\cdot\frac{20}{\sqrt{100}}=142\pm5.15=(136.85,\,147.15)\). "99% confidence" means: if this process were repeated many times, 99% of the intervals produced would contain the true \(\mu\).
questions.explanation: \(142\pm2.576\cdot\frac{20}{\sqrt{100}}=142\pm5.15=(136.85,\,147.15)\). "99% confidence" means: if this process were repeated many times, 99% of the intervals produced would contain the true \(\mu\).

questions.q: Consider the points \(A(1, 2, 3)\), \(B(2, 4, 1)\), and \(C(-1, 0, 5)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Find a non-zero vector \(\mathbf{n}\) normal to the plane containing \(A, B, C\), and write the Cartesian equation of the plane.
questions.answer: Step 1: Form vectors \(\vec{AB}\) and \(\vec{AC}\): \(\vec{AB} = \langle 2 - 1, 4 - 2, 1 - 3 \rangle = \langle 1, 2, -2 \rangle.\) \(\vec{AC} = \langle -1 - 1, 0 - 2, 5 - 3 \rangle = \langle -2, -2, 2 \rangle.\) Step 2: Compute normal vector via cross product: \(\mathbf{n} = \vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = \left|\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k} ; 1, 2, -2 ; -2, -2, 2\right| = \mathbf{i}(4 - 4) - \mathbf{j}(2 - 4) + \mathbf{k}(-2 - (-4)) = 0\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k} = \langle 0, 2, 2 \rangle.\) Simplifying by scalar factor 2 gives normal \(\mathbf{n}' = \langle 0, 1, 1 \rangle\). Step 3: Formulate plane equation using point \(A(1, 2, 3)\): \(0(x - 1) + 1(y - 2) + 1(z - 3) = 0 \Rightarrow y - 2 + z - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow y + z = 5. \quad \blacksquare\)
questions.explanation: Step 1: Form vectors \(\vec{AB}\) and \(\vec{AC}\): \(\vec{AB} = \langle 2 - 1, 4 - 2, 1 - 3 \rangle = \langle 1, 2, -2 \rangle.\) \(\vec{AC} = \langle -1 - 1, 0 - 2, 5 - 3 \rangle = \langle -2, -2, 2 \rangle.\) Step 2: Compute normal vector via cross product: \(\mathbf{n} = \vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = \left|\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k} ; 1, 2, -2 ; -2, -2, 2\right| = \mathbf{i}(4 - 4) - \mathbf{j}(2 - 4) + \mathbf{k}(-2 - (-4)) = 0\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k} = \langle 0, 2, 2 \rangle.\) Simplifying by scalar factor 2 gives normal \(\mathbf{n}' = \langle 0, 1, 1 \rangle\). Step 3: Formulate plane equation using point \(A(1, 2, 3)\): \(0(x - 1) + 1(y - 2) + 1(z - 3) = 0 \Rightarrow y - 2 + z - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow y + z = 5. \quad \blacksquare\)

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Level 3 · Advanced Find the extreme values of \(f(x, y) = x^2 + 2y^2\) on the circle constraint \(g(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 = 1\) using the Method of Lagrange Multipliers.
questions.answer: Set up Lagrange system \(abla f = \lambda abla g\): \(abla f = \langle 2x, 4y \rangle\), \(abla g = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle\). 1) \(2x = 2\lambda x \Rightarrow 2x(1 - \lambda) = 0\) 2) \(4y = 2\lambda y \Rightarrow 2y(2 - \lambda) = 0\) 3) \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\) From (1), either \(x = 0\) or \(\lambda = 1\): • If \(x = 0\): from constraint (3), \(y^2 = 1 \Rightarrow y = \pm 1\). Points: \((0, 1)\) and \((0, -1)\). Value: \(f(0, \pm 1) = 0 + 2(1)^2 = 2\). • If \(\lambda = 1\): from (2), \(2y(2 - 1) = 2y = 0 \Rightarrow y = 0\). From constraint (3), \(x^2 = 1 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1\). Points: \((1, 0)\) and \((-1, 0)\). Value: \(f(\pm 1, 0) = (\pm 1)^2 + 0 = 1\). Conclusion: The maximum value is \(2\) at \((0, \pm 1)\), and the minimum value is \(1\) at \((\pm 1, 0)\).
questions.explanation: Set up Lagrange system \(abla f = \lambda abla g\): \(abla f = \langle 2x, 4y \rangle\), \(abla g = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle\). 1) \(2x = 2\lambda x \Rightarrow 2x(1 - \lambda) = 0\) 2) \(4y = 2\lambda y \Rightarrow 2y(2 - \lambda) = 0\) 3) \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\) From (1), either \(x = 0\) or \(\lambda = 1\): • If \(x = 0\): from constraint (3), \(y^2 = 1 \Rightarrow y = \pm 1\). Points: \((0, 1)\) and \((0, -1)\). Value: \(f(0, \pm 1) = 0 + 2(1)^2 = 2\). • If \(\lambda = 1\): from (2), \(2y(2 - 1) = 2y = 0 \Rightarrow y = 0\). From constraint (3), \(x^2 = 1 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1\). Points: \((1, 0)\) and \((-1, 0)\). Value: \(f(\pm 1, 0) = (\pm 1)^2 + 0 = 1\). Conclusion: The maximum value is \(2\) at \((0, \pm 1)\), and the minimum value is \(1\) at \((\pm 1, 0)\).

questions.q: Solve \( |x + 3| = |2x + 6| \). Give the largest solution.
questions.answer: **Answer:** A. Working through this functions step: \( \text{Case 1: }x + 3=2x + 6.\ \text{Case 2: }x + 3=-(2x + 6).\text{ Largest solution: }x=-3 \) [M1] [A1]

questions.q: Calculate \( f^{-1}(x) \) if \( f(x) = \dfrac{3}{x} \).
questions.answer: **Answer:** A. Working through this functions step: \( y=\dfrac{3}{x} \Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3}{y} \Rightarrow f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{3}{x}\text{ (self-inverse)} \) [M1] [A1]

questions.q: Find the oblique asymptote of \( f(x) = \dfrac{2x^{2} + 9x + 8}{(x + 4)} \), in the form \(y=mx+c\).
questions.answer: **Answer:** C. Working through this functions step: \( \text{Dividing: }\dfrac{2x^{2} + 9x + 8}{(x + 4)} = 2x + 1 + \dfrac{4}{(x + 4)}\text{, so the asymptote is }y=2x + 1. \) [M1] [A1]
questions.explanation: Working through this functions step: \( \text{Dividing: }\dfrac{2x^{2} + 9x + 8}{(x + 4)} = 2x + 1 + \dfrac{4}{(x + 4)}\text{, so the asymptote is }y=2x + 1. \) [M1] [A1]

questions.q: Level 3 · Advanced Evaluate the improper integral or establish its divergence: \(\int_0^\infty x e^{-x/2}\,dx\)
questions.answer: Express as a limit of a definite integral: \(\int_0^\infty x e^{-x/2}\,dx = \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \int_0^t x e^{-x/2}\,dx\) Integrate by parts on \([0, t]\): Let \(u = x \Rightarrow du = dx\), and \(dv = e^{-x/2}dx \Rightarrow v = -2e^{-x/2}\). \(\int_0^t x e^{-x/2}\,dx = \left[ -2x e^{-x/2} \right]_0^t - \int_0^t (-2e^{-x/2})\,dx = -2t e^{-t/2} + 0 + 2 \left[ -2e^{-x/2} \right]_0^t\) \(= -2t e^{-t/2} - 4(e^{-t/2} - 1) = 4 - e^{-t/2}(2t + 4)\) Take the limit as \(t \rightarrow \infty\): By L'Hôpital's Rule, \(\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2t+4}{e^{t/2}} = \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2}{\frac{1}{2}e^{t/2}} = 0\). Therefore: \(\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} [4 - e^{-t/2}(2t + 4)] = 4 - 0 = 4\)
questions.explanation: Express as a limit of a definite integral: \(\int_0^\infty x e^{-x/2}\,dx = \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \int_0^t x e^{-x/2}\,dx\) Integrate by parts on \([0, t]\): Let \(u = x \Rightarrow du = dx\), and \(dv = e^{-x/2}dx \Rightarrow v = -2e^{-x/2}\). \(\int_0^t x e^{-x/2}\,dx = \left[ -2x e^{-x/2} \right]_0^t - \int_0^t (-2e^{-x/2})\,dx = -2t e^{-t/2} + 0 + 2 \left[ -2e^{-x/2} \right]_0^t\) \(= -2t e^{-t/2} - 4(e^{-t/2} - 1) = 4 - e^{-t/2}(2t + 4)\) Take the limit as \(t \rightarrow \infty\): By L'Hôpital's Rule, \(\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2t+4}{e^{t/2}} = \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2}{\frac{1}{2}e^{t/2}} = 0\). Therefore: \(\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} [4 - e^{-t/2}(2t + 4)] = 4 - 0 = 4\)

questions.q: Level 3 · Advanced Find the full interval of convergence (including endpoint behavior) for the power series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(2x - 1)^n}{n^2 \cdot 4^n}\).
questions.answer: Apply the Ratio Test: \(L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{(2x - 1)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^2 4^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n^2 4^n}{(2x - 1)^n} \right| = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{|2x - 1|}{4} = \frac{|2x - 1|}{4}\) Require \(x\): \(2x - 1 = 4\), giving \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{4^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\), which converges by the \(p\)-series test (\(p = 2 > 1\)). Endpoint \(x = -3/2\): \(2x - 1 = -4\), giving \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-4)^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\), which converges absolutely (since \(\sum 1/n^2\) converges). Therefore, the interval of convergence is \(\left[ -\frac{3}{2}, \frac{5}{2} \right]\).
questions.explanation: Apply the Ratio Test: \(L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{(2x - 1)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^2 4^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n^2 4^n}{(2x - 1)^n} \right| = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{|2x - 1|}{4} = \frac{|2x - 1|}{4}\) Require \(x\): \(2x - 1 = 4\), giving \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{4^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\), which converges by the \(p\)-series test (\(p = 2 > 1\)). Endpoint \(x = -3/2\): \(2x - 1 = -4\), giving \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-4)^n}{n^2 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\), which converges absolutely (since \(\sum 1/n^2\) converges). Therefore, the interval of convergence is \(\left[ -\frac{3}{2}, \frac{5}{2} \right]\).

questions.q: Use the substitution \(u = 2x + 1\) to find the exact value of \(\int_0^4 \frac{x}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\,dx\).
questions.answer: Let \(u = 2x + 1\), so \(du = 2\,dx \Rightarrow dx = \frac{1}{2}\,du\), and \(x = \frac{u - 1}{2}\). Change limits: \(x = 0 \Rightarrow u = 1,\quad x = 4 \Rightarrow u = 9\) Transform the integral: \(\int_0^4 \frac{x}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\,dx = \int_1^9 \frac{\frac{u - 1}{2}}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\,du = \frac{1}{4}\int_1^9 \left(u^{1/2} - u^{-1/2}\right)\,du\) \(= \frac{1}{4}\left[ \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} - 2u^{1/2} \right]_1^9 = \frac{1}{4}\left( \left(\frac{2}{3}(27) - 2(3)\right) - \left(\frac{2}{3}(1) - 2(1)\right) \right)\) \(= \frac{1}{4}\left( (18 - 6) - \left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) \right) = \frac{1}{4}\left(12 + \frac{4}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{40}{3}\right) = \frac{10}{3}\)
questions.explanation: Let \(u = 2x + 1\), so \(du = 2\,dx \Rightarrow dx = \frac{1}{2}\,du\), and \(x = \frac{u - 1}{2}\). Change limits: \(x = 0 \Rightarrow u = 1,\quad x = 4 \Rightarrow u = 9\) Transform the integral: \(\int_0^4 \frac{x}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\,dx = \int_1^9 \frac{\frac{u - 1}{2}}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\,du = \frac{1}{4}\int_1^9 \left(u^{1/2} - u^{-1/2}\right)\,du\) \(= \frac{1}{4}\left[ \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} - 2u^{1/2} \right]_1^9 = \frac{1}{4}\left( \left(\frac{2}{3}(27) - 2(3)\right) - \left(\frac{2}{3}(1) - 2(1)\right) \right)\) \(= \frac{1}{4}\left( (18 - 6) - \left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) \right) = \frac{1}{4}\left(12 + \frac{4}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{40}{3}\right) = \frac{10}{3}\)

questions.q: A random variable \(X\) has distribution \(\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\). A single observation of \(X\) is taken to test \(H_0: \lambda = 6\) against \(H_1: \lambda < 6\) at the 5% level. (a) Find the critical region. (b) State the actual significance level. (c) Find the probability of a Type II error if the true value of \(\lambda\) is 3.
questions.answer: (a) Under \(H_0\), \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(6)\). Calculate cumulative probabilities: \(P(X = 0) = e^{-6} \approx 0.00248\) \(P(X \leq 1) = e^{-6}(1 + 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.01735\) \(P(X \leq 2) = e^{-6}(1 + 6 + 18) = 25e^{-6} \approx 0.06197\) Since \(P(X \leq 1) 0.05\), the critical region is \(X \leq 1\) (i.e. \(X = 0\) or \(1\)). (b) Actual significance level = \(P(X \leq 1 \mid \lambda = 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.0174\) (or 1.74%). (c) Type II error occurs when we fail to reject \(H_0\) when \(\lambda = 3\). We fail to reject when \(X \geq 2\): \(P(X \geq 2 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - P(X \leq 1 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - e^{-3}(1 + 3) = 1 - 4e^{-3} \approx 1 - 0.1991 = 0.801\mathrm{\ (3\ s.f.)}\)
questions.explanation: (a) Under \(H_0\), \(X \sim \mathrm{Po}(6)\). Calculate cumulative probabilities: \(P(X = 0) = e^{-6} \approx 0.00248\) \(P(X \leq 1) = e^{-6}(1 + 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.01735\) \(P(X \leq 2) = e^{-6}(1 + 6 + 18) = 25e^{-6} \approx 0.06197\) Since \(P(X \leq 1) 0.05\), the critical region is \(X \leq 1\) (i.e. \(X = 0\) or \(1\)). (b) Actual significance level = \(P(X \leq 1 \mid \lambda = 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.0174\) (or 1.74%). (c) Type II error occurs when we fail to reject \(H_0\) when \(\lambda = 3\). We fail to reject when \(X \geq 2\): \(P(X \geq 2 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - P(X \leq 1 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - e^{-3}(1 + 3) = 1 - 4e^{-3} \approx 1 - 0.1991 = 0.801\mathrm{\ (3\ s.f.)}\)

questions.q: Solve the quadratic equation \(2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0\) by completing the square. State the vertex of the corresponding parabola \(y = 2x^2 - 5x - 3\).
questions.cross_lesson: 3.02 Lines and Planes in Three Dimensions
questions.answer: Factor 2 from the first two terms: \(2\left(x^2 - \frac{5}{2}x\right) - 3 = 0\). Halve the coefficient of \(x\): \(\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{5}{2}\right) = -\frac{5}{4}\). Complete the square: \(2\left(x - \frac{5}{4}\right)^2 - 2\left(\frac{25}{16}\right) - 3 = 0\Rightarrow 2\left(x - \frac{5}{4}\right)^2 - \frac{25}{8} - \frac{24}{8} = 0\Rightarrow 2\left(x - \frac{5}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{49}{8}\). Divide by 2: \(\left(x - \frac{5}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{49}{16}\). Take square roots: \(x - \frac{5}{4} = \pm\frac{7}{4}\Rightarrow x = \frac{5+7}{4} = 3\) or \(x = \frac{5-7}{4} = -\frac{1}{2}\). The vertex is \(\left(\frac{5}{4}, -\frac{49}{8}\right) = (1.25, -6.125)\).

The vertex is \(\left(\frac{5}{4}, -\frac{49}{8}\right) = (1.25, -6.125)\).

questions.q: Find all vertical, horizontal, and slant asymptotes and any removable discontinuities (holes) of the rational function \(f(x) = \frac{3x^2 + 1}{x^2 - 4}\). Describe its end behavior using limits.
questions.answer: Step 1: Domain and vertical asymptotes: The denominator factors as \(x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)\). The numerator \(3x^2 + 1 > 0\) has no real zeros. Thus, there are no common factors and no removable holes. The vertical asymptotes are \(x = 2\) and \(x = -2\). Step 2: Horizontal asymptote and end behavior: Numerator and denominator have equal degree \(n = d = 2\): \(\lim_{x \rightarrow \pm\infty} f(x) = \lim_{x \rightarrow \pm\infty} \frac{3 + 1/x^2}{1 - 4/x^2} = \frac{3}{1} = 3.\) The horizontal asymptote is \(y = 3\). Notice that for all \(|x| > 2\), \(f(x) = 3 + \frac{13}{x^2 - 4} > 3\), so the graph approaches \(y = 3\) from above as \(x \rightarrow \pm\infty\).

questions.q: Level 3 · Advanced A particle moves along a curve defined parametrically by \(x = t^2 + 1\) and \(y = t^3 - 3t\). Find the value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(t = 2\) and determine whether the curve is concave up or concave down at this point.
questions.answer: First find the components: \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 3t^2 - 3\). The first derivative is \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2 - 3}{2t} = \frac{3}{2}t - \frac{3}{2t}\). Differentiating with respect to \(t\): \(\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = \frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{2t^2}\). Then \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}(dy/dx)}{dx/dt} = \frac{\frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{2t^2}}{2t}\). At \(t = 2\): numerator is \(\frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{8} = \frac{15}{8}\); denominator is \(2(2) = 4\). Thus \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{15/8}{4} = \frac{15}{32}\). Because \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{15}{32} > 0\), the trajectory is strictly concave up at \(t = 2\).
questions.explanation: First find the components: \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 3t^2 - 3\). The first derivative is \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2 - 3}{2t} = \frac{3}{2}t - \frac{3}{2t}\). Differentiating with respect to \(t\): \(\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = \frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{2t^2}\). Then \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}(dy/dx)}{dx/dt} = \frac{\frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{2t^2}}{2t}\). Because \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{15}{32} > 0\), the trajectory is strictly concave up at \(t = 2\).

questions.q: The circle \(C\) has equation \(x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0\). (a) Find the coordinates of the centre and the exact radius of \(C\). (b) Find the equation of the tangent to \(C\) at the point \(P(6, 2)\).
questions.answer: (a) Complete the squares for \(x\) and \(y\): \((x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 + 4y + 4) = 12 + 9 + 4 \Rightarrow (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25\) The centre is \((3, -2)\) and the radius is \(\sqrt{25} = 5\). (b) The gradient of the radius from centre \((3, -2)\) to \(P(6, 2)\) is: \(m_{\mathrm{rad}} = \frac{2 - (-2)}{6 - 3} = \frac{4}{3}\) The tangent is perpendicular to the radius, so its gradient is \(m_{\mathrm{tan}} = -\frac{3}{4}\). Using point-slope form with \(P(6, 2)\): \(y - 2 = -\frac{3}{4}(x - 6) \Rightarrow 4(y - 2) = -3(x - 6) \Rightarrow 4y - 8 = -3x + 18 \Rightarrow 3x + 4y - 26 = 0\) In slope-intercept form: \(y = -\frac{3}{4}x + \frac{13}{2}\).
questions.explanation: (a) Complete the squares for \(x\) and \(y\): \((x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 + 4y + 4) = 12 + 9 + 4 \Rightarrow (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25\) The centre is \((3, -2)\) and the radius is \(\sqrt{25} = 5\). Using point-slope form with \(P(6, 2)\): \(y - 2 = -\frac{3}{4}(x - 6) \Rightarrow 4(y - 2) = -3(x - 6) \Rightarrow 4y - 8 = -3x + 18 \Rightarrow 3x + 4y - 26 = 0\) In slope-intercept form: \(y = -\frac{3}{4}x + \frac{13}{2}\).

questions.q: Which statement correctly conveys the meaning of a '95% confidence level'?
choices: If many random samples are drawn and intervals constructed, \(95\%\) of them will contain the true population parameter
There is a \(95\%\) probability that the true parameter lies inside the specific interval \([47, 53]\)
\(95\%\) of sample data values lie between \(47\) and \(53\)
The sample mean has a \(95\%\) chance of being correct
questions.answer: The confidence level describes the long-run coverage rate of the interval estimation process over repeated random sampling.
questions.explanation: The confidence level describes the long-run coverage rate of the interval estimation process over repeated random sampling.

questions.q: If a \(95\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is \([102, 118]\), what is the conclusion for the two-tailed test \(H_0: \mu = 100\) vs \(H_1: \mu \neq 100\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\)?
choices: Reject \(H_0\) at the \(5\%\) level, because \(100\) lies outside the \(95\%\) confidence interval
Fail to reject \(H_0\), because \(100\) is close to \(102\)
The test is inconclusive without a P-value
questions.answer: A hypothesized value outside a \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval is rejected at significance level \(\alpha\) in a two-tailed test.
questions.explanation: A hypothesized value outside a \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval is rejected at significance level \(\alpha\) in a two-tailed test.

questions.q: What happens to the width of a confidence interval if the confidence level is increased from \(90\%\) to \(99\%\) (with sample size fixed)?

questions.answer: Higher confidence requires capturing a larger portion of the sampling distribution, which increases the critical value and widens the margin of error.
